findings.title: Every managed request and heartbeat is serialized behind one global queue and synchronous state-file fsync
findings.description: The adapter keeps one process-wide `stateQueue` promise chain and every `mutateState()` call ends with `persistState()`, which uses synchronous `mkdirSync` plus `writeFileAtomicSync`. `stcontrolRequestTracker()` awaits that mutation before the request is admitted, then schedules another queued mutation on `finish`/`close`; login and `/api/users/heartbeat` use the same path. This makes all stcontrol-tracked requests contend on one synchronous disk-backed critical section instead of per-session state.
findings.snippet: let stateQueue = Promise.resolve(); ... async function mutateState(mutator) { const run = stateQueue.then(async () => { const state = loadStateSync(); const result = await mutator(state); persistState(state); return result; }); ... }
findings.recommendation: Remove synchronous disk I/O from the request hot path. Keep request accounting in memory or in a per-session/per-user lock, batch durable snapshots asynchronously, and avoid a single global queue for unrelated users. At minimum, `/api/users/heartbeat` and request in-flight counters should not require a process-wide fsync before `next()` runs.
findings.impact: This creates head-of-line blocking across unrelated users. At the default 2 minute foreground heartbeat, 1,000 active managed pages already generate a steady stream of queued fsync-backed mutations before counting normal reads and writes, and any slow disk flush delays all other tracked sessions because they share the same global queue.

findings.title: Controller disaster backup retries never get re-claimed after a transient failure
findings.description: The reconciler only calls `executeControllerBackup()` when `ScheduleControllerDisasterBackup()` returns a brand-new run. But `ScheduleControllerDisasterBackup()` treats any row in `retry_wait` as already covered and returns nil, while `FailControllerDisasterBackup()` moves transient failures into `retry_wait` and there is no other caller that claims existing runs. A failed backup therefore consumes the scheduler slot indefinitely instead of being retried after backoff.
findings.snippet: run, err := s.Store.ScheduleControllerDisasterBackup(...); if err != nil || run == nil { return }; if err := s.executeControllerBackup(ctx, run); err != nil { return }
findings.recommendation: Split scheduling from execution. On each reconciler pass, first claim any existing `scheduled` or due `retry_wait` run whose lease is absent/expired, then schedule a new run only when no runnable backup exists. The claim query also needs a due-time/lease-expiry predicate so retry backoff and worker restart recovery are actually honored.
findings.impact: One transient pg_dump, target-prepare, transfer, or publish failure can stall controller own-state backups indefinitely, because the scheduler never reaches the existing `retry_wait` row again and also refuses to create a replacement run while that row exists. Backup throughput drops to zero until manual cleanup changes the database state.

findings.title: Controller backup hashing reads the entire archive into memory before upload
findings.description: After building the backup archive on disk, the controller computes its digest with `os.ReadFile()` and `sha256.Sum256(data)`, which materializes the full tar.zst in RAM. The transfer path then opens and streams the same file again. Because the shared snapshot limit is 100 GiB, a full pg_dump-style controller backup can turn one backup pass into a very large one-shot memory spike and heavy GC pressure.
findings.snippet: func controllerFileSHA256(path string) (string, error) { data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return "", err }; sum := sha256.Sum256(data); return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]), nil }
findings.recommendation: Hash the archive as a stream, either while writing the tar.zst or by reopening it with `io.Copy(hash, file)` instead of `os.ReadFile`. That keeps memory bounded regardless of backup size and lets backup concurrency scale without full-archive heap copies.
findings.impact: Large controller backups pay for the archive three times: write to disk, full-file read into RAM for hashing, then upload streaming. That needlessly inflates peak RSS during backup windows and reduces how safely the system can run pg_dump backups alongside other controller work.

cross_references.reason: The same global serialized session-state path also creates the lease-admission race already flagged in architecture.
The stalled retry path is the concrete scheduler consequence of the recovery/scheduling boundary issue in controller backup orchestration.
